title: Three access exercises for Project 1
introduction: This week, Miha asked us to turn the question around. The Access Rider at the start of term was about what I need; this workshop was about whether my own work is accessible to audiences and collaborators. There were three exercises: language and understanding, intersectional difficulties, and physical access. I completed them for Project 1, the two-player picture book driven by hand signs.
related_work:
Language and understanding: three challenges

1. Translation. My mother tongue is Chinese, so most of my work goes through translation. I first formulate my thoughts in Chinese and then turn them into English; in this process, some meanings are altered or lost, whether in my texts, when I explain my work, or when I receive feedback.

2. Cultural gap. My practice carries a Chinese way of thinking and our own cultural references, from the images I choose to the way a story is told. Project 1 is based on made-up childhood memories, so certain scenes may not land for a UK or international audience: they may be unable to step into the scene or understand what it is saying.

3. Understanding without words. My work makes almost no use of words. Project 1 communicates through hand signs and pixel images; consequently, the audience must first learn its rules: what each hand sign means, what a scene stands for, and how rock, paper, scissors drives the story forward. Without any instructions, some people may not understand how to join in.
method:
Intersectional: who may receive the work differently

All my work so far is screen-based: pixel-art web pieces, and now an interactive piece controlled by hand signs (Project 1). Three groups may receive it differently.

Culture. The scenes in Project 1 depict a Chinese childhood: a courtyard wall, watermelon seeds, a blackout night, and a removal van in an alley. Audiences in the UK or elsewhere may never have lived those scenes, so they watch rather than remember. What I can do is keep the feelings universal (winning, losing, a friend moving away) and let the background carry the place rather than the story.

Family background. Some players may have had no childhood friend, or may have memories they do not want back. A piece about ‘remembering a friend’ can hurt. I will state at the outset that this is a story we are offering, not their memory, and that nothing they do is recorded.

My position. As I write from a Chinese position in a UK classroom, what feels nostalgic to me may read as exotic to others. I will ask classmates from other countries to test the piece and tell me which scene they cannot read, then change that scene first.
results_discussion:
Physical access: barriers, what I can do, how I will say it

Barriers. The piece needs a webcam and a second computer with a second person; two usable hands and enough room to move an arm; sight, because it is screen-only; English for the written lines; a quiet, well-lit space so that the hand tracking works; and a browser with a network connection to our server.

What I can do. Keep the number keys 1, 2 and 3 as an alternative to hand signs. Make the recognition tolerant: count extended fingers rather than requiring an exact shape. Provide the lines in both Chinese and English. Add the recorded voice lines so that the dialogue can be heard as well as read. Offer a single-player mode with a simulated partner. Show one hint picture of the three signs on the first screen.

How I will say it. A short access note on the first screen and on the website: what you need (a camera, your hands, some light), what you can use instead (the keys), what is not yet solved (there is no screen-reader version and no audio description of the pictures), and where it runs (any laptop with a browser; in class, two laptops facing each other). Miha’s point about managing expectations is the one I take with me: I cannot remove every barrier, but I can say honestly which ones are still there.
